I don't know of any pix, but there are a couple of telltale signs. If the top or
bottom of the lytic is bulging quite a lot, or if the splits in the metal
casing, usually on the top, are either oozing a sap-like substanceor they seem
too far apart (they should be touching each other). These are signs of a lytic
gone bad. If left too long, you'll hear a big BANG and then you'll see tiny bits
on aluminum foil everywhere. The lytic has exploded. It is quite unnerving to
hear/see it happen. If the lytic doesn't seem right to you, you are better off
replacing it. make sure the values AND physical size are the same. Most newer
lyrics are smaller, but the don't have all of the characteristics of the old
ones and could cause trouble down the line.

Ken

9005:
Anyone who uses MESS much is probably aware of the longstanding and very annoying "Out of timers" bug.  This has occurred ever since the MESS Astrocade driver switched to sharing the MAME Astrocade code.  When running Astrocade BASIC and related cartridges like the BASIC-carts, MESS immediately crashes with an "Out of timers" message.  After a lot of discussion on the MESS message boards, and at least one false start, I have managed to fix this crash.

The problem actually traced back to the MAME video code itself, video/astrocde.c.  MAME uses something called timers in order set up a function call for a specific time, such as the end of a scanline or the end of vblank.  The Astrocade video code uses a timer on every single scanline, expiring at the end of that scanline.  One of the things this timer does is to check for certain flags, and if they're met, call a function called astrocade_trigger_lightpen().  This function, in turn, checks some flags, and under certain conditions will set up a different timer.  Crucially, this timer was set to expire at the end of vblank.  Herein lies the problem.  If the proper conditions were met, then on every single scanline, the code would set up a timer that wouldn't expire until the end of vblank.  In MAME, this didn't turn out to be too bad.  Many games didn't check the lightpen ports at all.  Gorf might call this function about 10 times per vblank. 
 But Astrocade BASIC ended up meeting the conditions and setting up this timer on EVERY SINGLE SCANLINE.  MAME allocates memory for timers at the very start, with MAX_TIMERS set to 256.  Astrocade BASIC quickly exceeded this number of timers, thus causing the crash.

With this understood, the fix was actually fairly simple.  Instead of having the lightpen timer expire at the end of vblank, I set it to expire at the end of the scanline, the same as the previous per-scanline timer was doing.  Everything in MAME and MESS that worked before continues to do so, and nothing crashes with the "Out of timers" error.  Astrocade BASIC appears to be usable, and I played the Candyman and Super Slope BASIC-carts.  For whatever reason, Road Toad still doesn't start a game, but at least it doesn't crash anymore.

Richard had mentioned some complications with the lightpen interrupts on the Astrocade, and I'm still not sure if this is all set up correctly.  Indeed, it would be difficult to test without actually trying to emulate a lightpen, which is probably fairly low on the emulation priority list.  He mentioned a Color Picker program in particular, and while this doesn't crash anymore, it also doesn't run properly.  So, we should keep in mind that there may be various obscure parts of the system that aren't working quite right.

Still, I'm pleased to say that the most obvious problem has been fixed.  My change made it into MAME version 0.139u1, and has been ported over to the current MESS code.  So, if you compile your own version of MESS from the public repository, you can pick this up right now.  It won't be in the official release until version 0.140.

Paul

When Richard encountered the "Out of timers" crash, he explained it as follows:

"A cause of
this
 is when the interrupt register $0E Hex is set to $18 for screen interrupts
PLUS
 the undocumented unclipped light pen interrupts seen in the following bitmask
:

        bit 0   - Light pen interrupt mode (see below)
        bit 1   - Light pen (visible area) interrupt enable
        bit 2   - Screen (at scanline set) interrupt mode
        bit 3   - Screen (at scanline set) interrupt enable
        bit 4   - Light pen (full screen) interrupt enable
and bits 5 to 7 - not used

where mode is 0 - to hold interrupt until Z-80 acknowledges it
 or mode equal 1 - to cancel interrupt after next instruction."

My fix didn't change the interrupt logic itself, just the duration of the timers.  Astrocade BASIC is triggering a lightpen timer on every single scanline, and this is because of the way that bitmask is set.  It is possible that there's a deeper emulation bug here, and Astrocade BASIC should be changing those bits at some point such that the timer wouldn't be triggered so often. 9008:
Here I am again! Hmmmm, light pens. Light pens work on the light generated from
the screen hitting a photocell. When the light hits the cell, it sends a signal
to the light pen jack. This is checked as to when the beam has crossed the
screen from left to right (Horizontal trace time) and where it was vertically.
Both are critical to obtain accurate sensing of the place the light pen is on
the screen. The main problem with most light pens made for the Bally(I have one
and Leroy Flamm had made one, I don't know who else had any except the guys from
Dave Nutting, Midway, and Action Graphics) is they were inherently slow, making
timing of the Horizontal portion hard to get right. There was always a
fudge-factor needed. If you wrote a BASIC program, forget it, the beam is long
gone by the time the BASIC had unpacked the command and then interpreted it. It
really needed to be written entirely in machine code. At the time, there were
very few people that knew enough about machine code to write a program that was
useful. Besides, people only wanted to play games (or so Bally thought).
I hope this helps somewhat.
Ken

I think that the 300-BAUD interface is attached to the light pen port just for power.  This is how the Bally's joystick ports look compared to the Atari:

        Bally/Astrocade                         Atari Standard
        Controller port                         Controller port

        1. NC (No Connection)                   1. Up
        2. Down                                 2. Down
        3. Left                                 3. Left
        4. Right                                4. Right
        5. Trigger                              5. Paddle Potentiometer B
        6. Up                                   6. Fire Button
        7. Potentiometer end                    7. +5v (Paddle end)
        8. Ground                               8. Ground
        9. 50K Potentiometer (Knob)             9. Paddle Potentiometer A

        DB9 Male Port:        DB9 Female Plug:
          1 2 3 4 5             5 4 3 2 1
           6 7 8 9               9 8 7 6

As you can see, the Bally's port does not supply any power at all (unlike the Atari's, which does supply 5 volts).

BTW, this information was taken straight form the Bally / Astrocade FAQ, which can be read here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/faqs/bally-astrocade_faq.txt

9018:
I don't know how many have been waiting with bated breath for news about 300 baud Astrocade programs, but I figure it's time for an update.  When last we left off, Ronaldo had discovered a very useful tool for cleaning up recordings--Casio Utilities.  We e-mailed back and forth with the author, Marcus van Cube, and he gave a few explanations and made a few improvements.  I believe we've reached the point now where, while Marcus is still available to answer questions, any further improvements will need to be done by the Astrocade community.

The current version of the program can be downloaded here:

http://www.mvcsys.de/download/casutil.zip

The official documentation is here:

http://www.mvcsys.de/doc/casioutil.html#mozTocId83898

Adam, this would be a good thing to add to the Astrocade Tape Archive Tools page.  It's GPL, so there should be no problem with distribution as long as the source code and license is included.

So, how do you use this program for Astrocade recordings, you may ask?  Two utilities are useful for Astrocade recordings--wav2wav, and wav2raw.  These should work with any recordings using the Kansas City Standard.  wav2wav makes a direct bit-for-bit copy of the original, just cleaned up into square waves so it should load and compress more easily.  This is great for keeping exact timing intact.  wav2raw is slightly more processed, recovering the data bytes.  From this, you can get a .prg/.bin file which could be converted to the actual source code by Ronaldo's tools.

wav2raw should be used as follows:

wav2raw.exe -b -PN1 -i input.wav output.bin

-b means we're decoding data bytes.  -i means to ignore parity and framing errors (the Astrocade doesn't even use parity).  -PN1 means one stop bit.  There are also two relevant environment variables.  You would set these from the command prompt before running the program.  WAVE_PHASE can be either 0, for standard, or 1 to invert the wave pattern.  I seemed to have better luck with 1, but it's worth trying both ways.

set WAVE_PHASE=1

WAVE_THRESHOLD determines the sensitivity to amplitude changes.  The core part of the program is determining when the amplitude crosses the center line of the waveform.  But maybe it just goes a little above or below it.  If it's too sensitive, it might be affected by random noise.  If it's not sensitive enough, it might miss real data.  The values vary from 0 to 100, with higher numbers being more sensitive.  I had good luck with

set WAVE_THRESHOLD=75

but this will vary from recording to recording.

There's not much to using wav2wav:

wav2wav input.wav output.wav

Keep in mind that you can still vary WAVE_PHASE and WAVE_THRESHOLD, though.

So, with that in mind, what are some of the problems we run into with 300 baud recordings?  If you zoom in on a waveform, you'll hopefully see a regular almost square wave pattern, with repeating patterns of either eight waves at a 2400 Hz frequency or four waves at a 1200 Hz frequency.  The worst thing that can happen is a dropout.  The pattern just breaks down at some point, becoming either silence or random noise.  There's a bit of redundancy built into the Kansas City Standard, but if a dropout goes on for very long, data loss is inevitable.  Bothersome, but more manageable, is amplitude variation, where the tape will be quiet in some areas and loud in others.  This is where the WAVE_THRESHOLD comes in handy.  If the tape is warped, you can also see it speeding up and slowing down, affecting the frequencies.  The utilities seem fairly robust against this, but it's something to keep in mind.

Probably the most important problem we noticed was bias.  The ideal waveform will be exactly centered, with the high amplitudes rising and the low amplitudes falling by the same amount.  But some recording didn't look like this at all.  We could see the amplitude rising and falling, but it would be off center.  Sometimes, in fact, peaks would never rise above the center, or troughs would never fall below the center.  This might occur in a low frequency wobbling pattern.  You could see the high frequency amplitude variation of the data pattern, but imposed on this would be a lower frequency pattern slowly moving the entire waveform up and down.  I credit Marcus for finding an easy way to counteract much of this effect--a high-pass filter.  A high-pass filter lets high frequency variation (the data pattern) pass through, but filters out lower frequency variations (the wobble).  One tape we saw lots of wobble on is a collection by Super Software.  By using Audacity to apply a high-pass filter of 2400Hz to the recording before using the utilities, I got dramatically improved, and sometimes flawless results.  For examples, this:

. SUPER CRAPS

   1 .
   2 .    3 . BY ROB ROSENHOUSE
   4 . FOR SUPER STEP ?RE
   5 .
   6 . (C) 1980?   7 .   8 .
   9 :RETURN ;NC=2a0;F?.?
  ??"# ERS (1  20 K=KP-48;??1)+(K>4)GOTO 20
  30 ?T=3;MU="Q";NT=0;FOR A=1;@(A)=50;NEXT A
  40
 100 FOR K;CY=-8×;CX=PRINT "PLA#2,?@(A
 2-8×K-7STEP -8;CY=Z

to this:

. SUPER CRAPS

   1 .
   2 . SUPER CRAPS
   3 . BY ROB ROSENHOUSE
   4 . FOR SUPER SOFTWARE
   5 .
   6 . (C) 1980
   7 .
   8 .
   9 :RETURN ;NT=0;BC=240;FC=174;CLEAR
  10 CY=0;PRINT "# OF PLAYERS (1-4)
  20 K=KP-48;IF (K<1)+(K>4)GOTO 20
  30 NT=3;MU="Q";NT=0;FOR A=1TO K;@(A)=50;NEXT A
  40 CLEAR
 100 FOR A=1TO K;CY=-8×A-7;CX=-70;PRINT "PLAYER ",#2,A,;CX=26;PRINT @(A);NEXT A

So, where do we go from here?  For one thing, I think it's time to start (gradually) cleaning up the recordings we've already got.  We can get easily loadable, massively compressible files, and extract the source code to .txt files in the process.  (Volunteers definitely welcome.)  In addition, I've got a lot of 300 baud tapes that either I had problems with before or I haven't looked at at all.  This is definitely a good time to put some more effort into those.

Looking ahead, perhaps there will be an opportunity to improve the tools to recover even more data.  Sometimes, the tools just stop at a certain point in the recording.  I'd like it to skip ahead until it could start processing again, and tell me the exact time in the file that it retrieved every character.  This way, we could really hone in on the problem area, and see if it was possible, either through examining the .wav file or the BASIC code, to determine what should have been there.  Perhaps even the automated processing has room for improvement.

The process is very much the same as scanning with a flatbed scanner, as this scanner IS a flatbed scanner with one BIG (thought seemingly minor) difference.  The glass that the book rests on goes nearly to the VERY edge of the
scanner.  I suppose that there is about a 1/4" piece of plastic between the glass and the side of the scanner.  This means that you no longer have to either: 1) remove the
binding to scan the book, or 2) worry about the
gray-not-too-well-scanned area that is very typical near the binding of a
 book.  This is great for me since I'm scanning in some very difficult to find library books.

Scan time doesn't take any less or any more time than using a regular flatbed scanner.  I just finished scanning in a ninety-page book and converting it to a cleaned-up PDF with bookmarks.  I am very picky about my scans (as anyone knows who has ever volunteered to scan material for me for Bally Alley).  I ended up cleaning up the edges of each page, plus devoting a substantial amount of time to cleaning up the front cover (which had stickers ALL over it, as typical library books do).  I'd say that, had I not worried about the clean-up, that I could have cut the scanning time in half.  So, I'd say you could scan about 100-120 pages/hour.

If you don't have a flatbed scanner already, then I recommend this purchase because this scanner can also be used as a regular flatbed scanner (although the scanner's bed is smaller than is typical).  If you already have a flatbed scanner, then I would just keep using that unless you plan to scan quite a few books.

Before I bought this scanner, I looked at purchasing the sort of book scanner that uses cameras above a v-shaped cradle that holds the book.  After reading about them, these book scanners sounded GREAT.  They can "scan" about 700 pages an hour (it just depends on how fast you can flip the pages).  The problem is, I never could find these for sale except for professional models meant for libraries and other such institutions that scans literally TONS of material.  If anyone knows of these sort of scanners meant for mere mortals, then please let me know.

There are DIY book scanners (that use a camera), but I never tried one of these before.  Here's an example of one of these:

http://www.instructables.com/id/New-Improved-Portable-Paperless-Digital-Copy-M/

If only one or a few books are going to be scanned then I'd just work around the limitations of a regular flatbed scanner.

9040:
A few weeks ago, I described the latest developments in 300 baud processing technology.  At that point, however, while I'd experimented with all of the tools, I hadn't used them on a large scale.  So, I decided to start with the works of W&W Software Sales.  W&W Software was a very early and prolific tape software company, with programming done by Bob Weber.  They released 9 compilation tapes with 5 programs each, along with a couple of bonus programs.  The first seven tapes (that's 35 programs) were released in 1979, with two more tapes coming in 1980.  These were later re-released for AstroBASIC, but there were no new releases, though Bob Weber would occasionally publish programs in the Arcadian.

I chose to start with W&W in part because I had access to a variety of sources.  I had purchased five of these compilation tapes a few years ago.  Adam had made recordings from Brett Bilbrey's old tape collection, with a number of W&W programs.  (Both Brett and Bob were part of the active Michigan Astrocade scene.)  There was also source code for several programs scanned (sometimes individually, sometimes from the Arcadian), and Mike White had sent us a few programs.

So, with this, I strove to restore as many W&W programs as possible.  I started with my own tapes, since I could make high quality recordings.  Most processed with the Casio utilities with no problems, and I was able to further improve the results by running the recordings through a high-pass filter.  I did notice, however, that for the high-pass filter to work, you must record without clipping.  This makes sense, since otherwise, information about low-frequency wobbles in the amplitude will be lost.  I had a recurring problem in Russian Roulette, but fortunately, this was also available from Brett's collection, and I was able to determine the correct fix.  So, I got all 26 programs from my tapes working great (tape 9 had the bonus program Air Traffic Controller).

I then moved on to the recordings from Brett's collection.  These were more troublesome, because the recordings were lower quality.  I've learned a lot about how to get good tape recordings since the days Adam recorded these.  Still, many ran with no difficulty.  As I got into the more noisy recordings, I actually found that KCS got better results than the Casio tools, at least for these recordings.  But both were useful.  Often, I would process a recording with each tool, convert them to .txt files, and diff the files to check for errors.  I could then construct a correct .txt file and use txt2prg to go back to a program file.  I quickly abandoned doing simple filtering of the recordings (which would preserve the timing) in favor of regenerating a .wav file from the binary data with KCS.  This isn't really an issue for the W&W programs, since they're not doing anything fancy.  Every program just loads some code, then runs.  I found that a delay of 35ms usually worked well with KCS, approximately keeping the original length of the recordings.  I did have a problem with Words of Wisdom, which has a long list of words, skipping some characters, and reverted back to 50ms for this one.

For the most part, the correct code was obvious.  Sampler #3 had the most problems, and was somewhat of a judgment call, but I believe I got it right, and certainly the program works fine.  One frustrating case was Enhanced Lunar Lander, where I found that the end of the program was cut off in the original recording.  Perhaps one day I'll look at this tape (now in Russ's possession) to see if this was a glitch in the recording, or if the tape itself is missing the data.  I've saved what there is and given it a bad dump flag.  It is possible to land, though I believe something else should probably happen after that.  The only program I had to type in from source code is Ancient Sumeria, one of the bonus programs.  I haven't typed in the Bob Weber programs from the Arcadian.

In the end, I was very successful, with 45 of the 47 Bally BASIC programs working.  The only program missing completely is Brain Buster from tape 6.  W&W also did a single program for the Blue RAM expansion, Bally Nuclear Power Plant, which isn't available.  By comparing duplicates from my collection and the recordings from Brett's collection, I found alternate versions of Othello and W&W Racetrack.  I also found that the version of Checkbook Balancer & Compound Interest now on-line is from the Arcadian, and is different from the one originally released on tape. 9042:
I've gotten at least a bit of a feel for how Bally BASIC loads programs.  I think that when it writes them to tape, there isn't an identical delay between each character, because programs with certain characteristics needed a longer delay added into KCS.  For example, Words Of Wisdom had line after line of words followed by RETURN.

1001 PRINT "SANITY",;RETURN
1002 PRINT "AGONY",;RETURN
1003 PRINT "DISTRUST",;RETURN
1004 PRINT "POLITICS",;RETURN
1005 PRINT "GREED",;RETURN
1006 PRINT "GLUTTONY",;RETURN
etc.

I could see that there was an extra delay after RETURN and the line break, and after awhile, it was like it couldn't keep up.  So maybe, when Bally BASIC is writing out a program, it only has something like a 35ms delay between S/A/N/I/T/Y, but after the RETURN {line break} the delay is longer.  This makes sense, since the Astrocade has to print out several characters, then scroll the screen.  And perhaps the interface can buffer a certain amount of data, but then starts dropping characters.  I suppose someone could examine the original recordings to confirm some of this.

What new features were you thinking of?  I'd like to see more detail about unrecognized characters.  These all show up as question marks right now (which is what you'd see when loading them into Bally BASIC).  But in case it's loading machine code or data, it would be good to see the actual value.  Maybe it could decode as {hex value} for example.  This would also make it obvious when a character is the actual question mark character, which is part of the character set, or something else.  Usually, of course, this is clear from the context.

Paul

9057:
Mike White and I agree on 2 things, 1) Astrobasic's I/O is not very good. and 2)
The recorder is the key. Some recorders will NOT give a good output, no matter
what you do.
C.J. is right, the MIC input is the best. That's what Astrobasic (and the
cassette interface) were made to use. You you have a Blue Ram? the I/O of the
Blue Ram is a good preamp. it's output is nearly 4 Vouts if you go thru it with
the switch in the LOAD position. put the output of the recorder into the MIC
input of the BR and the computers AUX into the output (ear) of the BR. Aux
inputs need at least 2 volts. MIC inputs (outputs) are in the millivolt region.
Yot may need to put a 10-50K pot in line with the AUX in for impedance matching.
Wire it like a rheostat. Adjust it for maximum clarity of signal.
Need further info, please ask.
Ken

I've just uploaded the latest batch of goodies to the FTP server.  Probably the biggest thing is the W&W Software programs, as described in a previous post.  These can completely replace the 300 baud recordings now on-line.

I also went through a little bit more of the Bob Fabris collection tapes.  I've got four 300 baud recordings (now digitally processed as well)--2000 AD by Ed Larkin (from the Arcadian), a version of Mueller's Arcadian Slot program modified by an unknown author (presumably this was submitted to the Arcadian, but never published), Joystick Checkout by Sebree's Computing (a simple program to test your joysticks), and Mazin by Dave Ibach.  Mazin is the most interesting program.  It's mostly in machine language, and generates a maze (similar to what you'd see in Amazing Maze) for the player to get through.  It keeps track of your time, and multiple players can compete for the best times.  As far as I can tell, it keeps going indefinitely, generating a new maze for each round.  I'm surprised that, as far as I can tell, this was never published.  There are two 2000 baud programs--Random Maze Generator by The Tiny Arcade (mazes were obviously popular), and Pac-Man by Dale Low.  Pac-Man, again, appears to be an unused Arcadian submission.  Dale Low was the programmer behind Astrogames, a tape company which unfortunately doesn't seem to have anything archived.  Astrogames published a game called Super-Pac, but I don't think this is the same thing.  I've also got scans of a few tapes.  Some, like the Graphics Minicourse, already have programs archived, but now we have a tape scan as well.

I was glad to hear back from Mike Peace that his kids dug through his attic and found some more WaveMakers instructions.  For the first time, we can see the instructions for games like Max (Robot From Space) and Lookout For The Bull.  There are also some alternate versions, including the color instructions for Guitar Course (we just had the old black and white style before), and different colored versions of Castle Of Horror and Monkey Jump. This may be a good opportunity to look at the organization of the WaveMakers instructions. uses 6 bits and a ground and +5V for the chips, so it needs 8 lines.

I read your comments over at GameGavel, Bill, and I disagree with your advice about opening this Bally Arcade package.  I DO agree with your reasoning for opening it though.  USING the console is the key to enjoying it, but I'm against opening  this box for several reasons:

1)  The Montgomery Ward version of the Bally Arcade seems to be the second-most-prone to failure version of the console.  This is second only to the very first version of the Bally Arcade (the version distributed by JS&A).  This may be simply be because it has more shielding than the Astrocade version (can someone verify this?).

2)  I've never heard of the Montgomery Ward version being sealed.  Does this mean that the BOX is sealed or that the console is still in the plastic?

3)  I've heard of many cases of brand new in-the-box Astrocades not working straight out of the box.  I think that this was most common when the console was distributed by JS&A (when the rumored return rate was about 30% or possible even higher). 

4)  I've never heard of a sealed Montgomery Ward Bally Arcade.  EVER.  I see unopened Astrocade versions of the console, but NEVER the earlier version.

If the package IS opened, then I recommend that the console itself is also opened immediately and the RF shielding then be removed.  Depending on which version of the shielding is in the console then this can be easy (little or no solder removal required) to time consuming (plenty of solder to be removed).  In the later case, removing the solder can be quite difficult because the RF shielding itself acts as a heat sink and dissipates the heat enough that the solder will not melt.  In this case using a solder gun, rather than a solder pen is required.  If that's not available, then I've used TWO soldering irons at once to get the job done (awkward but doable).

I'd love to see high-quality versions of this box.  All of the pictures of the Montgomery Ward boxes that I've seen are rather beat up.

Back in the mid-nineties I came across a surplus store here in Albuquerque.  This is not your average "store."  The place is actually a huge warehouse that was (and continues to be) in complete disarray.  There is also a HUGE outside area.  Most of the stuff is electronics surplus from the local Air Force base.  In one overcrowded area was a large box that was about three feet square.  It was FILLED to the brim with new, sealed Astrocade Hand-Controllers.  These were NOT in boxes.  These must have been surplus controllers that were packed in the Astrocade boxes.  I would guess that there must have been literally hundreds of hand controllers in there.

I picked out four controllers for myself.  Hardly anything in this store has a marked price.  I asked how much they wanted for the controllers: $10 a piece.  That price wasn't bad (even back then).  However, I passed.  I would visit that place now and then and eventually, toward the end of the nineties, the box was gone.  Inventory is continuously coming into that place and there is hardly any room as it is, so I suspect that they were all thrown away.

As an aside, the UNCOVERED outside area of this surplus store also holds electronics.  I've come across many weird and wonderful old computers out there that were ruined.  Probably the strangest (and by far the BIGGEST) item that I ever saw there was the entire workings from a plant that created wafers for computer chips.  I'm not sure why it was stored outside, but it was completely ruined.  Also, another unusual item that I saw there was a rack-mounted Apple II.  The rack was obviously used for some scientific purposes.  Every slot in the Apple computer was filled with a card that had many cords coming out of it.  It looked like an octopus.

By far though, my favorite item at this store was a control board with MANY, MANY switches on it (like something I imagine you might have seen at Cape Canaveral many years ago).  Two switches, each under a plastic cover, was labeled.  One was marked, "Missiles Ready" and the other was marked "Missiles Away."  I have a feeling that it wasn't some rare controller for Atari's Missile Command.  That was a controller for the REAL Missile Command played by the government!

government!

9097:
I hooked up the VIPER expansion again this weekend to try to answer Adam's questions a little better.  I can definitely see the advantages to typing on a keyboard like this, and they made sure to make all of the BASIC functions available, including small and large type and keywords like INPUT and SNAP.  Even those four weird graphical characters are worked in there.  The keyboard itself works well, but definitely doesn't feel like a modern computer keyboard.  It reminds me more of a typewriter.  The keys are fairly heavy, and make a fairly loud click when you press them.  You also can't enter a character multiple times by holding it down.  You have to release it and then press it again.  Except, there is actually a REPEAT key.  When you hold this down, you can press another key down and have it keep inputting as long as you hold both keys down.  This makes a rather loud clicking from the keyboard, and I find it difficult to control how many times you input a character, as the keyboard gets ahead of the screen, and after you release the keys, characters keep appearing for awhile afterward.

What is problematic is that they clearly used a standard key set rather than designing something specifically for the system.  So, for example, you have a key labeled with } and ], but you're not able to actually type a }, because it's not part of the character set.  Push the key by itself, and you get ].  Push it with SHIFT, and you get SNAP.  This is another problem.  While the keywords are available, they aren't labeled in any way.  To really start typing in programs quickly, you would need to memorize several combinations.  The same thing goes for less standard characters.  The ^ key gets you an up arrow (which at least matches somewhat).

I was surprised that the letter keys default not to the letters, but to keywords and such.  Pushing just H gets you LIST.  SHIFT and H gets you H.  It is possible to type in characters more quickly by pushing down CAPS LOCK (the key on the keyboard actually stays depressed until you push it again).  But then you have to release CAPS LOCK to enter a keyword.  Holding down shift while CAPS LOCK is depressed won't have any effect on the letter keys.  CAPS LOCK/SHIFT/H is still H.  CAPS LOCK has no effect on the non-letter keys, and SHIFT will continue to work with these as usual.  The key to switch between small and large type is actually a completely unlabeled key on the lower-left corner.

Now, can you load a driver and use the keyboard with Bally BASIC or AstroBASIC?  A few years ago, at the CinciClassic convention, Matthew Knapp and I archived a 300 baud Blue RAM keyboard driver, and tested it with his Blue RAM expansion.  I know we were able to use his keyboard, but my memory fails me on the exact details of what we did.  I did work some with the General Video Assembler, an AstroBASIC program, so perhaps I was able to use it with this somehow, loading the driver through the 300 baud input on the Blue RAM.  I'm not certain, though.  Does anyone know in more detail what BASIC versions the keyboards were compatible with, and what was required to activate them?  In any case, I tried loading this driver into Bally BASIC, and while it did load some recognizable code, I couldn't actually get the keyboard to work.  I also tried using :INPUT in AstroBASIC to load this into the 300 baud interface, and not surprisingly, this had absolutely no effect.

Paul

I've always preferred the versions of the program that ARE separated so that they don't have to be loaded from the menu.  While I think it's kinda neat that you try to get these programs to load as they were originally intended, I feel that the authors surely would have avoided this tedious loading process if they could have avoided it (except for George Moses, whose music programs ran one right after the other without user intervention).

There are three ways to load an Astrocade program:

1)  Tape - Loading one program into RAM and then running it is the normal method to use a tape program.  The program has to be "cued up" to the programs beginning tone and the it will load.  The various menus were created as a means to avoid needed to "cue up" a program.

2)  Tape (via a menu) - Load a menu (the first program on a tape) and then the menu automatically chooses the right program from the tape and then loads it.  If the menu has eight choices, and you choose choice number eight, then you have to wait while the menu passes the first seven programs.  For AstroBASIC, that's about two minutes and twenty seconds before program eight is reached (presuming there is no silent space between each "track," which there WOULD be), plus twenty seconds to load the program.  That's about a three minute wait.  That's QUITE a time consuming process.  This method might have been okay in 1982 (maybe-- but probably not!) when you're using 2000-BAUD, but it falls apart at 300-BAUD.  It's just TOO slow.  Now that any program can be loaded directly from a computer I don't understand the purpose of digitally archiving the METHOD that the tape used to load the program.


3)  Cartridge - This is the preferred method for loading BASIC programs.  A cartridge that loads a BASIC program is called a BASICart.  This is how the BASIC programs on the multicarts all load.  This is by far the easiest method to load a BASIC program.

I recommend that you don't worry about the WAY that a program loads.  What does it matter if the original loading method is still usable as long as the program can be run?  Then, of course, there is the other problem with the D&D program for the Astrocade.  It doesn't support the new 4'th edition rules... or even the second edition rules from 1989...  Maybe we should write to the author for an update. ;-)

Adam
9108:
I guess we're getting into the question of why, exactly we want to archive these programs.  One obvious reason is the for the fun of actually playing them.  For some programs, that makes a lot of sense.  For the Dungeons & Dragons package, it's not a game, just some tools for character generation and such.  While it might have at least been useful at one point, it's unlikely anyone will seriously use it to help their roleplaying nowadays.  But there is, I think, a second reason to archive programs, which is more formal historical preservation.  People may wonder (indeed, I wondered when I heard about it)--how did Dungeons & Dragons utility programs work in 1980?  As it turns out, part of the answer is that you may wait 20 minutes to load one.  (Hopefully, they used this time to flesh out their character's backstory.)  So I do, when possible, like to closely replicate the original format.  But, with the tools we have now, it's easy enough to do both.  I've decided I can just keep the filtered version of the raw recording (even if I can't get the loading program working, since indeed I don't care to spend any more time on that), and offer separated programs as well.

Paul

FILE SEARCH  It is possible to have the Bally look for a specific program
on tape and load only that program when it gets to it. Programs of any
kind on a tape or disc are usually called "files" in big machine-talk,
and are either titled or numbered. On the Apple, for example, you can
call a file "george" and ask the computer to "RUN GEORGE" from disc, and
it will search for george, load it, and then run it. On the Tektronics,
it would be numbered, and you'd enter "FIND 6/LOAD/RUN" to do the same
thing. Well, in studying the Tiny Basic listing, Al Rathmell found that
the Arcade will do the same thing. His report follows:    "To make use of the file finding capability of Basic, a file number
    must be written on tape when the file is created. The number is a
    16 bit (two 8-bit bytes) integer, and can have any value from -32768
    to + 32767, but for simplicity, if the high order byte (the first
    one) is always zero, then file numbers from 0 to 255 can be written
    in the low order byte. The two file number bytes are written in the
    proper format using the TV instruction. For example, to write a
    program on tape as file number 10, use the following command:
        :PRINT ;TV=0;TV= 10;LIST
    The first TV instruction writes the high order byte (zero), and the
    second TV instruction writes the low order byte (ten). To read file
    number 10 into the Bally, use the following command:
        :INPUT 10
    The file finding system also works with the :LIST and :RUN commands.
    Using the file numbering capability of Bally Basic adds a professional
    touch to tape file management!"

Of course it works, just enter up to FIFTEEN characters from the
name of the program, at a minimum enter these "shortcut" names :

 'C' for CLERICS & DRUIDS - the only single character string
 "MAG" for MAGIC-USER & ILLUSIONIST - there's a MA in "MAKER"
 "FI" for FIGHTERS - because there's already an F in "LAWFUL"
 "TH" for THIEVES & ASSASSINS - since variable 'T' is used
 "PER" for PERSONALITY - since there is a PE in "SPELLS"
 "RACE" for RACES - since there is RAC in "CHARACTER MAKER"

Would a list of programs on the Search page helped? Yes!
Would a "Select 1-6" menu be better? Sure, definately
Had the program ID words gone un-used? Well, yeah...
Is there any tape error detection? No, sorry Ken

Anyone that released a program that works gets my respect.

Of course it dumped the 8 into charisma.  The two-byte keys, while clearly present and unusable, did not interfere with the loading program.

So, I'll amend my statement.  We learn that sometimes, people released software with unused portions that they probably never expected anyone to be looking closely enough to find.  Perhaps Rich Tietjens intended to use the Arcadian-style program, but changed his mind for some reason.  Or maybe he was just trying to confuse future software archivists.  :-)

But to answer Adam, sometimes really buggy software did make it out the door.  I've seen on two tapes now a 300 baud WaveMakers Fortune Teller that, despite saying to pull the trigger for another fortune, actually just gives two fortunes immediately, then crashes.

In any case, I'm glad we figured this D&D program out.  But I will still make some separated versions as well for easy loading.  I'm also glad to be able to take care of so many programs with one tape.  Mike White's software list devotes 11 entries to this one.

Paul

Differences between Bally BASIC Manual versions 1 and 2

On page 2 they removed "All Rights Reserved" in the newer version

Pg. 3 Index - added sub-chapter page numbers and more appendixes.

Pg. 8 Overlay LETTERS - The 'slash' was correctly colored in red.

Pg. 9 - as Paul noted, they added an additional sentence = "Don't
hold down the shift key when you press a letter or character key"

Pg. 11 add "Never spell out computer words like B-O-X or S-T-E-P,
      use the gold WORDS shift key to enter these computer command
      words into your program." followed by a table of...
           RUN    STEP   RND
           LIST   NEXT   GOTO
           FOR    GOSB   INPUT
           TO     RETN   PRINT  (they left out a few) and...
    "A complete description of these Computer Command words is on
    page 122." followed by a box that said "Note: If your computer
    says WHAT? you have made an incorrect entry.  The computer
    will point out the mistake with a question mark (?).
    Correct that line only."

Pg. 12 - add after "HELLO!" - "The quotation marks are important
   because only the letters you put between them will be printed."

Pg. 13 (after "...number it 20.") "Notice that GOTO is one word."
Instead of "Check your program and see if it matches the example"
uses "Notice how line 20 tells the computer to go to line 10 and
print HELLO! again."  Both variations continue "If your TV screen
doesn't match this picture," - but "RESET your computer and enter
line number 10 and line number 20 again." is replaced by simply:
"fix the entire line that has the mistake by reentering the line
number and the correct line."

Pg. 16 changed (press the WORDS key before you press) GO to GO+10
"Be careful to use the letter X not the multiplication sign (x)."

Pg. 17 changed another (after "Or press WORDS and") GO into GO+10


PROGRAMMING COURSE pages have TABs with LESSON number 1-8 on them

Pg. 52 - replaced wrong code "S" with "$" as seen in screenshot.

Pg. 60 - changed IF K=30 to IF K=31 for ERASE key's return code.

Pg. 63 - inserted (computer) "draws the cursor box and" (waits),
     and also changed another Key 30 to 31 for "is the erase key."

Pg. 64 Screen size was only 159 by 87 instead of 160 by 88 dots!


PROGRAMS | COMPUTER GAMES | PHASER PHUN program listing on...
Pg. 99 - added missing line "190 GOTO 10" to make it loop right!!

Pg. 102 ROCK/SHEAR/PAPER listing was missing even more lines...
  280 H=H+1
  290 GOTO 30
  301 PRINT "ROCK";RETURN
  302 PRINT "SHEARS";RETURN
  303 PRINT "PAPER";RETURN

Pgs. 107-110  corrected some music scores for the PLAYER PIANO:
   including Melody / March / Marine's Hymn / Stars and Stripes -
   and also added vertical lines between columns of musical notes.


APPENDIX Terms and Symbols | Computer Words section...
Pg. 122 - changed "ERASE: means forget the last key you pushed."
      into "ERASE: means remove the last item you entered."

Pg. 128 - took out "Control Words" (for 300 baud tape) section
      and moved the old "Arithmetic" section up from page 129

Pg. 129 - new "Keypad Inputs" and "Music Synthesizer" sections

Pg. 130 - expands old "Control Words" into "Audio Tape Control"
      section - adding a picture  and "With the Bally BASIC audio
      cassette interface accessory you can store programs on audio
      tape, play Bally software cassettes and exchange pro- grams
      over the phone."  (Did anybody manage to make a MODEM work?)

      about the latest Bally BASIC software and accessoties, see
      your Bally dealer or write:
           Bally BASIC
           Bally Consumer Products Division
           10750 West Grand Ave., Franklin Park, Ill 60131"

The BACK COVER had the BALLY(R) logo with "PROFESSIONAL ARCADE",
      "FUN & BRAINS tm", the address again, and an ISDN number:
      "0620 00304-A0000 1078", plus "Printed in U.S.A." as well.

"permission was given to change it over to the Bally hand control, but the expert assigned drug his feet and an amateur (me) had to do it!"  An Astrocade cart list says a cartridge titled "Missile
Attack" was projected for release in 1983.  And Brett himself wrote in the Michigan Astrobugs Newsletter JUL.82 pg.3, "I've been hired recently to design new cartridges for Astrocade, Inc.  Currently, I am responsible for the new Missile Attack cartridge (#2020).

http://www.ballyalley.com/newsletters/astrobugs/astrobugs_newsletter_july_1982-original.pdf

But apparently, Mike wasn't writing about Brett.  In message #96, he says, "I was told to
modify I.C.B.M Attack for the Bally joysticks as Don Gladden [of New Image
software] drug his feet and didn't do it."

I asked Brett about this more recently, but he didn't remember working on a conversion, or giving permission for Astrocade to do it (though admittedly, it's been a long time).

Did Astrocade, Inc. make some sort of deal to modify and distribute ICBM Attack?

How did this job get assigned to Don Gladden?  How did it then come to Mike?

Now, on to Muncher.  I'd be interested to learn more, if he knows, about how this ended up being sold through the Arcadian.  There are some interesting hints in Bob Fabris' recorded conversations with Ed Larkin, who was manufacturing the carts.  Was Astrocade Inc. ever
going to try to sell it, or were there just too many legal difficulties?
Someone bought a prototype "Munchie" cart from a former Astrocade employee, who

As for Quest For The Orb, there aren't a lot of good sources for it, but there is a really nice flyer here:

9134:
While our initial discussion was to convert the I.C.B.M. Attack cartridge to work with a normal handle, the cartridge that "Action Graphics" wanted me to work on first was the "defenders" game. It was partially done, and needed someone to finish it. Sadly, I wrote games in Z80, and they wanted me to program in Terse Fourth using their UV-1 development systems. They shipped a UV-1 to me, and said, "go finish the game". If only they had let me do the I.C.B.M. Attack cartridge conversion...

As you might imagine, trying to do the defenders game on the UV-1 did not end well. Someone else eventually did the game and did a pretty good job...

As to allowing someone else to modify I.C.B.M. Attack for a normal handle, I would have had no problem with that, and simply don't remember if I said go ahead or not. But if Astrocade was going to do it and release it commercially, then I would have wanted some royalty, and that was never discussed.

By the time others were getting involved and discussing modifying I.C.B.M. Attack, I had already moved on and was working at Frederiksen and Shu Labs.

Bottom line, Astrocade never approached me about rights to sell I.C.B.M. Attack commercially. But then again, not everything they did was above boards...

Brett

9141:
lucifershalo wrote:
>>
same with
SKUNK

it says
switch to AB then press =
>>

You will find this to be the case with all of the game's that were on Mike White's multicarts (the very first multicart for the Astrocade... from 1990!).  This is also the case with games that were originally tape games and then moved onto cartridges (these sort of cartridges are referred to as BASICarts).  Here is what is going on:

1) You insert the cart

2) The BASIC game loads into RAM

3) The loaded program is put into a loop waiting for a key to be pressed.

4) You put Blue Ram BASIC or AstroBASIC into the cartridge port either by removing the multicart and putting in the actual BASIC cart needed or by switching the multicart's switches to the correct position on your sheet that came with your multicart.  Removing a cartridge while the system is ON is pretty unusual, but the Astrocade was designed to allow this to happen (although normally you scramble the RAM-- but the special loop that the Astrocade is running allows the RAM to stay "safe").

5) You press the button that the screen asks you to press.

6) Your program starts.

You will find that games that use AstroBASIC are limited to two colors on-screen at once (usually, but not ALWAYS true).  Blue RAM BASIC allows four colors (or is it eight?).  Either way, you're playing games written in BASIC that are usually much more limited than a cartridge game written in machine language.  Still, without this seemingly convoluted method of loading these games, then the only way to play these games would be to load them from a tape.

9143:
I didn't realize until after I replied to Laurent's email that it was a personal email. I figured that I'd send it to the group as there is some information in here that is worth sharing with everyone.

Laurent wrote:
>>
for smash up
when u say to set the multicart to that program
you mean blue ram basic
>>

I can't recall. I think that there is a version for both versions of BASIC, but I'm not sure if they are on the Multicart. Either way, try AstroBASIC. If that doesn't work, then try Blue Ram BASIC 1.1. You can't hurt anything by trying the wrong one.

>>
I dont need to push reset?
>>

No. Don't press Reset. That will erase RAM, and you DON'T want to do that. The point of BASICarts (even when they are on the multicart) is that they allow RAM to not become corrupted when cartridges are changed.

Swapping cartridges and saving RAM contents was SO important, that in 1982 there were a series of articles in the Arcadian newsletter called "Cartridge Conversion" (AKA BASIC Cartridge Swapping) that took advantage of this. These articles explained how to swap the Bally BASIC and Astrobasic cartridges while the machine is still on without losing the data. This would allow you, for instance, to load 300 baud programs into Bally BASIC, swap with the AstroBasic cartridge, and then save at 2000 baud. This is VERY useful for archive purposes. Also, at the time it was written it was used to load 2000-BAUD programs into Bally BASIC and then print them. The routine that is discussed is EASY to use, but a discussion of how it works (with ML source) is probably overkill for most of us. In 2002 I typed these articles up and they can all be read here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/basic/Cartridge_Conversion.txt

>>
if I want to change for another game
can I change the position of the switches and push reset
does that damage the console?
>>

This won't hurt anything. The current game that you are playing will stop working until you press Reset and start the new game, but you are not hurting the console. This is, in face, how I use my multicarts.

>>
how do I know the programs that are using basic?
>>

If the games require BASIC then you'll be prompted to switch switches around, or to insert BASIC. If you need to switch switches around, then ignore the switch pattern on the screen (it was used when the games were no on the newer multicarts). If you need to "insert" BASIC, then you can just adjust the switches on your multicart to use whichever version is required.

>>
sorry for all those newbie questions
>>

These are hardly newbie questions. There are FEW multicarts around, so there really isn't any other place to get this sort of information.

I hope that you're enjoying your multicart!

Adam

like INPUT and SNAP.  Even those four weird graphical characters are
worked in there.  The keyboard itself works well, but definitely doesn't
feel like a modern computer keyboard.  It reminds me more of a
typewriter.  The keys are fairly heavy, and make a fairly loud click
when you press them.  You also can't enter a character multiple times by
holding it down.  You have to release it and then press it again.
Except, there is actually a REPEAT key.  When you hold this down, you
can press another key down and have it keep inputting as long as you
hold both keys down.  This makes a rather loud clicking from the
keyboard, and I find it difficult to control how many times you input a
character, as the keyboard gets ahead of the screen, and after you
release the keys, characters keep appearing for awhile afterward.
>
> What is problematic is that they clearly used a standard key set
rather than designing something specifically for the system.  So, for
example, you have a key labeled with } and ], but you're not able to
actually type a }, because it's not part of the character set.  Push the
key by itself, and you get ].  Push it with SHIFT, and you get SNAP.
This is another problem.  While the keywords are available, they aren't
labeled in any way.  To really start typing in programs quickly, you
would need to memorize several combinations.  The same thing goes for
less standard characters.  The ^ key gets you an up arrow (which at
least matches somewhat).

to keywords and such.  Pushing just H gets you LIST.  SHIFT and H gets
you H.  It is possible to type in characters more quickly by pushing
down CAPS LOCK (the key on the keyboard actually stays depressed until
you push it again).  But then you have to release CAPS LOCK to enter a
keyword.  Holding down shift while CAPS LOCK is depressed won't have any
effect on the letter keys.  CAPS LOCK/SHIFT/H is still H.  CAPS LOCK has
no effect on the non-letter keys, and SHIFT will continue to work with
these as usual.  The key to switch between small and large type is
actually a completely unlabeled key on the lower-left corner.

First, what's required to use this.  Besides a working Bally and/or
Astrocade unit...

A.) BALLY Basic cartridge (not the one labeled "Bally Basic" with a
cassette jack built-in, that's actually the same as the "Astro Basic"
that came later.)

B.) the Audio Cassette Interface jacked into Joystick #3 and the Light
Pen port

C.) connected to either a cassette recorder, a CD player or a PC's sound
card MIC and speaker connections

D.) and this WAV file copied to a cassette tape, CD or onto your PC hard
drive.

E.) a Blue Ram memory device (any size) plugged into the expansion port.

F.) a Blue Ram keyboard connected to the ZIF socket of the Blue Ram.

and G.) some reason to even want to program in Basic using a keyboard.

Assuming you have all of those, just use the keypad to load this driver
and you will then be able to use the keyboard instead!
If I remember right, I used to have to think "Capital A" to remember to
use the Shift key when entering letters.  Since the command WORDs are
assigned to the lower case ASCII values, that is what you get without
shifting.

driver, as long as you (or a program) don't enter ":RETURN" - turn it
back on with "CALL28416;&(14)=8;NT=3" (or re-load the driver) if it

9157:
Part 2.)
You can use a look-up table and convert all the lower-case letters (in
the output of WAV2RAW) into Basic WORDs, and the ASCII 13's into
carriage returns [c/r]'s, then read what would be displayed on-screen.
Luckily, there is a program that will do that for you...

Thanks to our Ronaldo, you can use PRG2TXT.EXE to transform KEYBOARD.PRG
into KEYBOARD.TXT (the extentions don't have to match the program name,
it just helps.)
Normally, this would be enough to read the program, as the line-numbers
are spelled out as digits, and lines actually end where they should.

Where there are no line numbers, the commands would be executed just as
if they had been entered from the keypad (and GO pressed).
Program listings do not need to appear in numerical order, and if a line
number is repeated only the last one is stored.  RUN needs to be entered
in order to run.

In this case, there are some ASCII 8 (BackSpace)'s mixed-in, which erase
just like hitting the ERASE key would.
But wait, what about that whole stretch that came out as errors (marked
by -->'s) or random charcaters/words...

There is a block of Z80 machine code which the loop in the first line
will intercept and save way up in extended memory.  It will not print to
the TV while the driver is loaded.
When that is done, the next character is a 'U' which is verified after
the loop.
[note: If the last line of your KEYBOARD.ASM is NOT a commented-out
definition of this as 01010101B please re-download KEYBOARD.ZIP - I made
some other changes!]

Finally, the last Basic line is read in and executed - turning off tape
reading, hooking the driver into the screen interrupts, disabling Light
Pen interrupts, and restoring NoteTimer.

Well, not exactly.  I believe my fix was correct as far as it goes. MESS shouldn't have been tracking the interrupts so long that it crashed.  But I don't understand the interrupt behavior well enough to know if that had been implemented correctly or not.  And I didn't even have a good test case for it.  There's no light pen emulation in the driver.  AstroBASIC seemed to work, but can't easily be too thoroughly tested without tape loading.

Richard sent me an interesting note about 300 baud loading:

"looking at the 300-baud tape readcharacter routine -
The "Audio Cassette Interface" sends out Light Pen Interrupts to mark at least four ones,
a zero or "start" bit, and 8 bits of ASCII, then kills time until the next character arrives.

These at-least-13-LPI's are repeated 300 times at a maximum - about 3900 per second,
which would be 65 per screen, or roughly once every 4 scanlines, so one/line is enough."

This tells me that proper light pen interrupt emulation may be needed to get 300 baud tape loading supported.

Your reason to use the calculator (it's onscreen memory, basically) is actually one of the better aspects of the Astrocade's calculator.

The reason I asked the question by the way is because I played "War" a LOT yesterday on my console (and I finally started to win some games).  I played "War" so much because I am trying to make the manual as
thorough as I can (not that the game really needs any explaining at
all).  I must have looked at the start menu, with "War" being the first choice dozens of times.  Of course, I couldn't help but notice the other built-in programs.  It got me to thinking about the other two non-games, Scribbling and Calculator.

While I was typing-in my notes for "War" into Notepad, I put Scribbling on 0 Players and just let it fill the screen with its screen saver-ish display.  I wondered if anyone else ever really did this back in the day.  Perhaps they put it on while a party was going on or something.  It still is pretty interesting to watch the random display, though it would have been much more impressive to see that filling the screen in 1978... long before anyone had ever heard of a screen saver or had seen a toaster with wings.

Then I started calculator and I wondered what kid would have used THIS program.  This program was really for adults only (not NC-17... just BORING to kids).  Though I do remember when I got my first hand-me-down calculator in the early eighties I used to play with it just for the heck of it.  It used a nine-volt battery and had red 7-segment displays.  It was quite a large monster.  Around this time I recall some kids in school having different books on Calculator Games.  I would borrow them and play around with them.  I recall one book by Scholastic (I think) being called something like "100 Calculator Games," but I looked it up on Amazon and didn't find it.  I guess armed with a book like this, an Astrocade and a rainy day (and no cartridges!) a kid could really have amused himself!

;-)

9202:
Having a lot of experience with electronics and the Bally system, It could be
almost anything wrong. From the power supply regulators to having had lightning
blow out some (or all ) chips, a bad Custom Chip, of a bad modulator. I don't
know if you have another Bally to swap parts with, but that is the best way to
check all replaceable parts. Other than that, you'll need some electronic test
equipment. Like volt - ohm meter, oscilloscope,  and maybe a digital circuit
analyzer.
I know this may not help you much, but the good news to think about is., SOme of
those parts can be replaced.
Ken Lill

9211:
Using a combination of a high-pass filter and the 300 baud processing tools has done wonders for the previously hopeless Super Software tapes in the Bob Fabris collection.  But with one program, Mystery Maze, I'm kind of wishing it hadn't.  :-p

For starters, both the program on the tape and the two listings available have a serious bug.  Line 100 reads:

100 M=JX(1)×2;N=JY(1)×2;IF (M=0)×(N=0)GOTO 130

The obvious problem with this is that line 130 doesn't exist.  Looking at the program, the most likely fix to me seemed to be changing it to GOTO 13000.  Does anyone have an alternate suggestion?  You can find the listing here:

http://www.ballyalley.com/type-in_programs/super_software/full_size/Mystery%20Maze%20%28Super%20Software%29%28BASIC%20Type-In%29%28with%20docs%29.pdf

Or:  http://tinyurl.com/2froop4

Line 13000 is the code for a game over from electrocution.  So, the effect of this modified line is that if you stop moving, even for an instant, you get electrocuted.  In theory, I can see how this would add an element of excitement to the game.  In practice, I found myself frequently dying from this when I tried to change directions.  Plus, you die instantly if you're not pushing on the joystick as soon as the program starts.  I'm not sure why they didn't just have you keep moving in one direction until you pushed another one, like in Checkmate.

On top of this, large swathes of the board randomly electrify and kill you.  There is, so far as I can tell, no way to avoid this fate.  With these two effects, I found that getting to the end of the maze was very unlikely.  After playing a number of times, I did finally reach the end of first maze, after which you get to do it again.  I've played some unfair and frustrating BASIC games before, but I think this one may take the prize.

9218:
You're right, Adam.  The program does immediately crash with an error on line 100.  The program Mystery Maze was commercially available.  There are ads for it in the Sourcebook.  However, I don't have one of the official tapes.  In Bob Fabris' tape collection, I found three hand-labeled tapes with a total of 18 Super Software programs on them.  These came along with source code listings from six programs.   Five of these were one the tapes, but one, Cosmic Zap, I only have the source code for.  So, I have access to 19 total programs, which is still less than half of what Super Software eventually released.  I would guess Super Software programmer Bob Rosenhouse sent these to Bob Fabris, but I can't be sure.  I have no way of knowing if this version of the program went to any paying customers, but I suppose it's possible he could have accidentally copied a work-in-progress version instead of the final version, or something along those lines. 
 There is actually a version number in the listing, so there could be a number of revisions out there.

I did get some sense of satisfaction when I finally finished my "advanced" version.  It's one of those things where I kept getting close, and I knew it should be possible to actually reach the end.  I wasn't always sure whether I was dying from random electrocution or from not moving.  Once I tried Lance's change, I finished the first maze on the first try, so it's clear that I was usually dying from not moving (even though I tried to change directions as quickly as possible).  Still, I don't like the game design.  The "maze" is so simple that's it's quite easy to navigate through.  So with just a little skill and practice, you'll get to the point where you'll die of random electrocution long before you run into a wall or run out of fuel.  And there are no lives.  When you die, it's an instant game over.  We do have instructions on one of the source listings, and it sounds like this is actually how it's supposed to play.  I doubt I'll bother
 with making a worst games list to go along with the best games list we've been talking about, but this one would certainly be a contender.

Paul

9219:
In the current issue of Retro Gamer (Issue 82) there is an article called "The Making of Gorf."  It's based on a new interview with Jamie Fenton.  It's a fun read, plus there is information that I didn't know.  For instance:


"We ended up hacking the [Bally Astrocade] custom chips and making them better [for Gorf].  That's where you get the 'sparkle': that twinkle in the shield on the first and fifth levels.  Then we had an effect that put stars on the screen just using one bit.  Those two cheap special effects were built into the hardware."


"That controller was taken from a B1 Bomber," adds Jamie.  "Dave Nutting based it on a design we had done for the defense industry way back in the beginning.  The pilot would press that red button to launch a nuclear device and then BANG!"


"Jamie still has the  [Ms. Gorf] development disks, bearing the legend 'RIP Ms. Gorf 6/82 - 8/83', and wistfully talks of revisiting the game someday."


[On Gorf's Galaxians Level] "Yeah, I spelt it wrong.  You make mistakes.  I mean, if someone had asked me at the time to spell Galaxian, I would have put an 's' on the end!  I made them vicious too.  It can get crazy but you can get through it.  I known Galaxian was the first game Bally lost the rights to make copies of, so I guess that's why it didn't make it into the home versions."


To order the current issue (the one with Mario on the cover), visit:

http://www.retrogamer.net/

This magazine is U.K. based, so if you live in the U.S. the magazine doesn't come cheap as shipping can be expensive.  Still, the whole magazine is a great read.  Classic Gamer is certainly the best classic gaming magazine that exists, though it can be a bit weird sometimes to read about computers and game consoles that were never released in the United States.

Thanks.  Most of that is because I got to used a computer and Bally and Astrocade had to literally cut and paste.  The computer allowed plenty of trial and error on my part.  Which is good, since this was my first experience doing anything like this.  If there is anyone to thank for the professional-looking layout, it is really Modern Computers and the information that they give access to.  The software that is available is amazing, but it also helped that I could use free PD artwork.
